solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Dirty books in second venue for literary festival

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for second
B is book, so two of them make the plural
Hay-on-Wye in Wales hosts a famous book festival

explanation.surface: Smutty books are on sale at the second site of a book festival.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hay Festival, held in the Welsh border town of Hay-on-Wye, is Britain's best-known literary festival; the books sit inside HAY, with S in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Shabby clothing or rooms are worn and grubby, so the word works as a loose synonym for unclean.

clue.text: Bag held up in Candide’s Act I, usually

indicators.note: something sitting in a run of words is contained by it, so the letters lie within the text
in a down clue, lifting something up turns the letters so they read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the name, the next two words and the start of the last

explanation.surface: A theatre note: a bag is lifted on stage in the first act of Candide, as a rule.
explanation.walkthrough: Read candidES ACT I USually backwards and SUITCASE appears; 'held up' reads naturally as a stage direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A suitcase is a travelling case for clothes, one particular kind of luggage carried by hand.

clue.text: Floating platform headed back to sailors

indicators.note: to head something here is to behead it, cutting off its first letter

blocks.note: a raft is a flat floating platform

explanation.surface: A raft drifts back towards a group of sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Headed' suggests steering somewhere, but here it means losing the head: RAFT without its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Aft is the nautical term for the rear or stern part of a ship, so seamen use it where others say back.

clue.text: Cowshed shelved, both unfinished and romantically moody

indicators.note: something unfinished lacks its ending, so each word drops its final letter

blocks.note: a byre is a cowshed
a plan that is shelved is put on ice

explanation.surface: A cowshed project has been shelved, left half-done, and its owner broods.
explanation.walkthrough: BYRE loses its E and ON ICE loses its E, then the two stumps join.
explanation.definitionFit: Byronic describes the brooding, passionate hero typical of the poet Lord Byron and his writing.

clue.text: Building’s top plant installer?

blocks.note: surface reading: the leading fitter of machinery in a construction firm
setter's reading: someone who lays reeds or straw on the roof of a building

explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' suggests industrial equipment and 'top' suggests the best, but the plants are reeds and the top is the roof.
explanation.definitionFit: A thatcher is the craftsman who covers roofs with straw, reed or other dried vegetation.

clue.text: It is a question of parentage

blocks.note: first meaning: a coy word for sex, as in 'doing it'
second meaning, taken literally: an enquiry after someone's dad

explanation.surface: A philosophical remark that something is really a matter of who one's parents are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' looks like a throwaway pronoun but is the first definition. The answer is a jokey British euphemism for sex that is literally phrased as a question about a father.
explanation.definitionFit: The humorous British phrase is a euphemism for sexual activity, and word for word it asks after a parent's wellbeing.

clue.text: Possible plagiarism involving Spanish article which is run without obstacles

indicators.note: to involve something is to include it, so one piece is taken inside another

blocks.note: plagiarism is stealing someone's words, a kind of theft
la is the feminine 'the' in Spanish

explanation.surface: A possible case of copying involves a Spanish newspaper article.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' looks like a piece of writing, which fits plagiarism, but it is the grammatical article. The flat is British horse racing without jumps.
explanation.definitionFit: Flat racing is the horse-racing season run on level courses, as opposed to National Hunt racing over hurdles and fences.

clue.text: Drove in rush, desperate to find water on Manhattan’s West Side

indicators.note: someone desperate acts wildly and out of order, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A thirsty driver rushes frantically across New York looking for water.
explanation.walkthrough: The first three words supply exactly the eleven letters needed; 'desperate' reads as the driver's mood.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hudson River flows along the western edge of Manhattan island, separating it from New Jersey.

clue.text: Power for line of forwards is rewarding

indicators.note: one thing given for another is exchanged for it, so a letter is swapped out

blocks.note: P is the symbol for power
L is the abbreviation for line
to forward a message is to relay it

explanation.surface: Sporting talk: giving the forward line more power pays off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line of forwards' looks like a rugby or football front line, but 'forwards' is a verb, RELAYS, whose L is swapped for P.
explanation.definitionFit: A task that repays effort gives something back in return, which is what being rewarding means.

clue.text: Not being satisfied about male campers, maybe, breaking record time

indicators.note: something that breaks into a thing splits it apart and sits within the gap

blocks.note: a disc is a gramophone record
on can mean concerning, as in a talk on birds
men sleeping in a tent could be called tent men
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Dissatisfied men at a campsite set a record time for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Record time' reads as one phrase, but its two pieces are split apart by the rest. 'Maybe' flags that campers are only one example of men in tents.
explanation.definitionFit: Discontentment is the state of unhappiness with one's situation, the noun matching a gerund phrase.

clue.text: Bury rival, small person applying for job?

blocks.note: to inter is to bury
to vie is to compete, to rival
wee is Scottish for small

explanation.surface: Ruthless advice: bury your rival, you little job seeker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small person' looks like one unit, but 'small' belongs to the wordplay and 'person applying for job' is the definition. The question mark admits not every applicant gets interviewed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is being interviewed is typically a candidate seeking employment, so this is a definition by example.

clue.text: Impertinence masked at the outset by daughter’s sauce

indicators.note: a mask covers the face, so hiding the start means the first letter is lost

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter
lip is cheeky talk

explanation.surface: A daughter's cheekiness is hidden at first behind her saucy manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sauce' looks like more cheek, echoing impertinence, but it is the food sense. LIP loses its L and follows D.
explanation.definitionFit: A dip is a thick savoury mixture into which crisps or vegetables are dunked, a kind of cold relish.

clue.text: Very serious man with stylish clothing

indicators.note: clothing wraps around a body, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: Ron is a man's name
chic means stylish

explanation.surface: A very solemn man in fashionable clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stylish clothing' looks like a noun phrase for his outfit, but 'clothing' is the verb: CHIC clothes RON.
explanation.definitionFit: In informal British speech chronic means dreadful or severe, as in a chronic shortage.

clue.text: Unruly spirit destroyed debt records

blocks.note: rum is a spirit
bust means broken or destroyed
an IOU is a written note of a debt

explanation.surface: A wild spirit tears up the records of what is owed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Destroyed' looks like an anagram signal but it gives BUST; IOU stands for 'I owe you'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rumbustious is a chiefly British word for boisterous and hard to control, close in sense to unruly.

clue.text: You, once humble, putting forward Liberal that’s a bit jaundiced?

indicators.note: moving something forward places it at the front, ahead of the rest

blocks.note: ye is the old form of you
L stands for Liberal
lowly means humble

explanation.surface: Once-humble you promoting a Liberal who is slightly cynical.
explanation.walkthrough: The humble word has two Ls; the Liberal is its second one, moved up to the front rather than a letter added from outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Jaundice turns the skin yellow, so someone slightly jaundiced has a yellowish tinge; the question mark admits the medical stretch.

clue.text: Electronic components cracked on some circuits and died, losing current

indicators.note: something cracked is broken apart, so the letters are rearranged
whatever is lost is taken away, so a letter drops out

blocks.note: taken as written
D is the abbreviation for died
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: Parts on some circuit boards cracked and failed after the power went off.
explanation.walkthrough: Add D to the three words, take away one I, and shuffle what remains. The electrical surface makes 'current' look literal.
explanation.definitionFit: Semiconductors are materials such as silicon used to make transistors and chips, basic parts of electronic devices.

clue.text: Slippery slope limiting America’s support

indicators.note: something slippery slides about and will not hold its place
to limit something is to set bounds around it, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: taken as written
the standard abbreviation for the United States of America

explanation.surface: A warning that the country's backing is on a slippery slope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slippery slope' reads as the familiar idiom, but the adjective is an instruction to jumble the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To espouse a cause is to adopt and champion it, so espousal is the backing given to it.

clue.text: One’s highly strung, which may describe spinal cord

blocks.note: first meaning: a very anxious, jumpy person
second meaning, taken literally: a tied-together mass of nerve fibres

explanation.walkthrough: 'Highly strung' also hints at strings tied up, and the second half takes the idiom literally as anatomy.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a person in a state of great nervous tension, while literally the spinal cord is a bundled mass of nerve tissue.

clue.text: Unsmiling principal brings in commercial parking

indicators.note: to bring something in is to take it inside, so a piece goes within another

blocks.note: a dean heads a college or faculty
an ad is a commercial
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: A stern head teacher introduces paid parking on the school grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Commercial' reads as an adjective describing the parking, but it is a noun, an advert.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadpan expression is deliberately blank, showing no amusement even when joking.

clue.text: European Court function is set up to protect voter

indicators.note: in a down clue, setting something up raises it, so it reads from the bottom upwards
protecting something means surrounding it with a shield, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: a role is a function
E is the abbreviation for European
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: The function of the European Court is to safeguard the individual voter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'European Court' looks like one institution, but the two abbreviations go in together, inside the other piece once it is turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: An elector is a person entitled to vote in an election, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Got Edward as a prize, as usual

blocks.note: to win a prize is to get it
surface padding that confirms the getting is winning
Ted is a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: Someone has won Edward as a prize, as they always do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As a prize' belongs to the first piece: one gets a prize by winning it.
explanation.definitionFit: Wonted is an old-fashioned adjective meaning customary or habitual, as in her wonted cheerfulness.

clue.text: Survive disembarking after everyone else?

blocks.note: someone disembarking is getting out
whoever comes after everyone else is last

explanation.surface: Staying alive by being the final passenger off the ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay also describes the answer: getting out last means outlasting the others, which the question mark hints at.
explanation.definitionFit: To outlast someone is to live or last longer than them, so it can stand for survive in a transitive sense.

clue.text: Hooter modified to cover front of brass instrument

indicators.note: something modified has been altered, so the letters change their order
whatever covers a thing lies over and around it, so one piece encloses another
the front of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A car horn has been adapted to cover the mouth of a brass instrument, like a mute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass instrument' wants to be the definition; 'brass' only supplies its first letter, and the instrument is a theorbo, a large bass lute.
explanation.definitionFit: A theorbo is a long-necked lute of the baroque period, a plucked string instrument used for continuo.

clue.text: Form of three-way junction without a coupling

blocks.note: a T-junction is a three-way road junction shaped like the letter
w/o is the written abbreviation for without

explanation.surface: Road engineering: a three-way junction built without any link between the roads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coupling' looks like a mechanical link between the roads, but it is a couple, a pair.
explanation.definitionFit: A couple or pairing is made up of two, so the number stands for a coupling.

clue.text: Drill bit with vertical grip?

blocks.note: surface reading: a boring tool's cutting piece with an upright handle
setter's reading: a part of military drill in which soldiers hold their rifles upright in front of them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drill bit' reads as the tool attachment, but drill is parade-ground drill and the bit is one move of it.
explanation.definitionFit: The command is a military salute where each soldier holds a rifle vertically in front of the body.

clue.text: Wish undone in French way

blocks.note: first meaning: to regret, wishing something had not happened
second meaning: the French word for a street

explanation.walkthrough: 'In French way' reads as 'in the French manner', but 'way' is a road.
explanation.definitionFit: To regret an action is to wish it undone, and a rue is a street in any French town.

clue.text: In study I messed up division

indicators.note: a thing messed up has been thrown into disorder, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A student confesses to getting the long division wrong while studying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Division' looks like maths homework, but it means disagreement, and 'In' is part of the letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Disunity is a lack of agreement within a group, the same as division among its members.

clue.text: Writer needing men in good health

blocks.note: OR stands for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers
someone in good health is well

explanation.surface: An author who needs his staff to stay fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a container signal, but 'in good health' is one piece; the men simply come first.
explanation.definitionFit: George Orwell was the English author of Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four.
